title: The Living God and Handmade Idols
overview: Jeremiah mocks idols made by human hands, praises the LORD as the maker of everything, and then mourns the coming exile of his people.

parts.label: Don't fear stars or statues (vv. 1-5)
parts.note: Neighboring peoples, especially the Babylonians, read eclipses and other sky events as omens and worshiped carved images. Jeremiah pictures an idol as a decorated log nailed in place so it won't topple, stiff like a scarecrow or a carved palm post (the Hebrew is unclear and translations differ), unable to speak, walk, help or harm.

parts.label: No one like the LORD (vv. 6-10)
parts.note: The poem turns to praise: the LORD is the true, living, everlasting King, unlike costly idols covered in imported silver and gold and dressed in royal blue and purple. Tarshish was probably in Spain, and Uphaz is unknown, possibly another name for the gold-rich land of Ophir.

parts.label: A one-line answer (v. 11)
parts.note: This verse is written in Aramaic, the common language of the Babylonian empire, as if giving Israel a ready reply to foreigners: gods that did not make heaven and earth will vanish. Scholars debate whether Jeremiah wrote it or it was added later, though it appears in all the oldest copies.

parts.label: Maker of all things (vv. 12-16)
parts.note: The LORD made the world and controls thunder, rain and wind, while idols have no breath and will be destroyed. Calling God the "Portion of Jacob" means he is Israel's share, what belongs to them, just as Israel belongs to him.

parts.label: Pack up, exile is coming (vv. 17-22)
parts.note: People in the besieged city are told to gather their belongings, because God will throw them out of the land and an army from the north, Babylon, will leave Judah's towns empty. The nation mourns like someone whose tent has collapsed and whose children are gone, and blames its leaders, the "shepherds," for not seeking God.

parts.label: A prayer for limits (vv. 23-25)
parts.note: Jeremiah, speaking for his people, admits humans cannot steer their own lives and asks God to correct them in measure, not in full anger. He ends by bluntly asking God to pour out his fury on the nations who have devoured Israel, words almost identical to Psalm 79.

think: What do people today rely on to feel safe or to predict their future, and how would you tell whether it is worth that trust?
